a: The rescue of that day
p: Teshu'ah means rescue. Many Bibles say "victory," which hides the link to David's song.
b: Teshu'ah is the ordinary Hebrew word for being rescued or saved. In a battle report it means a victory, and many translations say so here. This translation keeps "rescue" so the reader can hear how often 2 Samuel 19–24 uses the word and its family: the troops' rescue turns to mourning (19:2), the LORD "won a great rescue" through David's warriors (23:10, 23:12), and David's song calls God "the rock that saves me" and the one who "makes great the rescues of his king" (22:3, 22:47, 22:51). The same root gives the names Joshua and Jesus ("the LORD saves").

a: My son Absalom! Absalom, my son! My son!
p: David's lament runs on from 18:33. Readers ask whether it is love to admire or a failure of duty.
b: David's cry repeats "my son" again and again, and the narrator gives it in full twice (18:33; 19:4). Many readers hear in it the most human moment in the book: the king, who would not mourn his first son after the child died (12:22–23), cannot stop mourning this one, though Absalom tried to kill him. On the rabbis' reading of the repeated "my son," see the note on 18:33. Other readers side with Joab: a king who mourns his enemy in public shames the men who died for him. The narrator gives no verdict; the next verses let Joab speak.

a: Today you have made the faces of all your servants burn with shame
p: Joab, who killed Absalom against orders, now tells the king the truth no one else will.
b: Joab killed Absalom against the king's plain order (18:5, 18:14). Now he scolds David with blunt words: you love those who hate you, and you would rather we all died. Readers judge him in different ways. Many see him as cruel but right: a king's grief cannot cancel the loyalty of his army, and Joab's threat (19:7) is a fair warning, not a coup. Others note that Joab is also protecting himself, and that he never admits his own part in the king's sorrow. David obeys him at once (19:8) but replaces him with Amasa (19:13), and on his deathbed he tells Solomon to deal with Joab (1 Kings 2:5–6).

a: speak to your servants' hearts
p: A Hebrew idiom for words that comfort, reassure or win someone over.
b: To "speak to the heart" of someone is to say something kind and reassuring to them. Shechem speaks to Dinah's heart (Genesis 34:3), Joseph to his frightened brothers (Genesis 50:21), Boaz to Ruth (Ruth 2:13), and God to Jerusalem at the end of the exile (Isaiah 40:2). Joab wants David to thank his men, not to give them orders.

a: sat down in the gate
p: The town gate was where leaders sat to judge and be seen. David's return to it is a return to rule.
b: Ancient Israelite gates were large buildings with rooms and benches on both sides of the passage, as excavations at Dan, Gezer and Megiddo show. Elders sat there to judge cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1), and kings sat there to hear the people. Absalom stole hearts by waiting at the gate to hear complaints (15:2–6); David sat "between the two gates" waiting for news of the battle (18:24). By sitting in the gate now, David shows himself to the troops as their king once more.

a: Speak to the elders of Judah
p: David's own tribe had backed Absalom's revolt. David now courts it with an appeal to kinship.
b: Absalom's revolt started in Hebron, the old capital of Judah (15:7–10), and Amasa, Absalom's general, was a Judahite and David's nephew (17:25). So Judah had good reason to fear David's return. The northern tribes moved first (19:9–10). David answers by sending the priests to shame Judah into acting ("why lag behind everyone?") and by offering Amasa Joab's job (19:13). The move wins Judah, but it angers the north (19:41–43) and sets up Sheba's revolt in the next chapter. Many historians see here the old fault line between Judah and the northern tribes that will split the kingdom after Solomon (1 Kings 12).

a: my own bone and flesh
p: The phrase means close kin. The northern tribes used it when they made David king (5:1).
b: "My bone and my flesh" is how Laban greets his nephew Jacob (Genesis 29:14), and how Abimelech appeals to his mother's clan (Judges 9:2). It reaches back to the first man's words about the woman: "bone from my bones / and flesh from my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). All Israel used the same words at Hebron to make David king (5:1). Now David uses them to win back Judah alone, and the northern tribes will feel left out (19:43).

a: God do this to me, and more besides
p: An oath formula: the speaker calls on God to punish him if he does not keep his word.
b: The Hebrew says, "So may God do to me, and so may he add." The speaker probably made a gesture to show what "this" meant, such as a cut throat. The formula binds a promise with a self-curse. Ruth uses it (Ruth 1:17), Eli (1 Samuel 3:17), Saul (1 Samuel 14:44) and David himself (3:9, 3:35). Here David puts his own life on the line to give Absalom's general the top command.
orig: כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה־לִּי אֱלֹהִים וְכֹה יוֹסִף (koh ya'aseh-li Elohim vekhoh yosif)

a: in Joab's place
p: David hands the army to the man who led Absalom's forces. Was it reconciliation, or revenge on Joab?
b: Amasa had commanded Absalom's army (17:25). Making him David's commander is a bold peace offer to the rebels and to Judah. It also punishes Joab, who had killed Absalom against orders (18:14) and had just spoken harshly to the king (19:5–7). Readers differ on which motive weighed more. The plan fails within days: Amasa is slow to gather Judah (20:5), and Joab kills him (20:10).

a: Shimei son of Gera hurried too
p: The man who cursed David and threw stones at him (16:5–13) now hurries to be first to beg forgiveness.
b: When David fled, Shimei of Saul's clan cursed him and threw stones at him (16:5–8; see the notes there). Now he hurries to be first at the river, and he brings a thousand Benjaminites with him. The crowd is a show of shame and also of strength: Benjamin, Saul's tribe, is watching how David treats its men. Sparing Shimei (19:23) is also a way of winning Benjamin back.

a: Of the whole house of Joseph
p: Shimei is a Benjaminite, yet he speaks for "the house of Joseph," a name for the northern tribes.
b: Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh were the largest northern tribes, so "house of Joseph" can stand for the whole north (Judges 1:22–23; 1 Kings 11:28; Amos 5:6). Benjamin, Joseph's full brother, belonged with them politically. Shimei claims to be the first of the north to come back to David, a sign of how quickly loyalty was shifting.

a: Shimei cursed the LORD's anointed
p: Abishai turns David's own principle around: cursing the LORD's anointed deserves death.
b: David twice refused to let Abishai kill Saul because Saul was "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 26:9). Now David is the anointed king, and Abishai uses the same title to argue that Shimei must die; the law forbids cursing a ruler (Exodus 22:28). The title "anointed" (Hebrew mashiach) is the word that later becomes "Messiah."

a: my adversary
p: The Hebrew word is satan, "adversary," here a human opponent. 1 Chronicles 21:1 uses it for the tempter.
b: David says the sons of Zeruiah have become his satan, someone who stands in his way. In the Hebrew Bible the word usually names an ordinary opponent: the Philistines fear David may become their satan in battle (1 Samuel 29:4), and God raises up adversaries against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14, 11:23). The angel who blocks Balaam's road is "a satan" (Numbers 22:22). Only in Job and Zechariah does "the satan" appear as an accuser in God's court (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1–2; Zechariah is after the exile, and the date of Job is debated), and 1 Chronicles 21:1 uses the word where 2 Samuel 24:1 names the LORD. See the note on 24:1.
r: 24:1; 1 Samuel 29:4; Numbers 22:22; 1 Kings 11:14; Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1

a: he gave him his oath on it
p: David swears not to kill Shimei, but on his deathbed he asks Solomon to see to Shimei's death.
b: On the day of his return David will not spoil the celebration with blood. Yet in 1 Kings 2:8–9 he reminds Solomon that he swore "by the LORD" not to put Shimei to death, and asks Solomon to bring him down to the grave in blood. Some readers defend David: he kept his oath in his lifetime, and Shimei remained a danger to the dynasty. Others see a king who keeps the letter of an oath and breaks its spirit. The rabbis debated the case; many modern commentators read 1 Kings 2 as a hard-edged political ending that the narrator does not hide.

a: Mephibosheth son of Saul
p: Mephibosheth is Saul's grandson, Jonathan's son. Hebrew "son" often means any descendant.
b: Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son, lame in both feet since a fall at age five (4:4), and David took him to eat at the king's table for Jonathan's sake (9:1–13). Calling him "son of Saul" here may also stress the point at issue: is he loyal to David, or does he hope for Saul's throne, as Ziba claimed (16:3)? In 1 Chronicles 8:34 his name is Merib-baal; many scholars think "bosheth" ("shame") replaced "baal" in names in Samuel.

a: Mephibosheth had not tended his feet or his mustache
p: Unwashed feet, an untrimmed mustache and dirty clothes were signs of mourning.
b: "Doing" the feet probably means washing and caring for them; "doing" the mustache means trimming it. Covering or neglecting the upper lip was a sign of grief (Leviticus 13:45; Ezekiel 24:17, 24:22; Micah 3:7). The narrator, not Mephibosheth, tells us that these signs lasted the whole time David was away. That detail is the strongest evidence that Mephibosheth was loyal and that Ziba's story in 16:3 was a lie, though some readers think the signs could have been staged.

a: my servant tricked me
p: Ziba had accused his master (16:3). Now Mephibosheth answers, and David never rules on who lied.
b: The question of who lied is set out in the note on 16:1. Chapter 19 adds Mephibosheth's own account: he meant to ride with the king, but being lame he needed the donkey to ride, and Ziba left without him and slandered him. Three things in this chapter lean toward believing him: the narrator's report that he mourned the whole time David was away (19:24), his refusal of any claim on the king (19:28), and his offer to give up the land (19:30). Readers who doubt him point out how skillfully he speaks and that he flatters the king. David does not decide; he splits the land (19:29).

a: you and Ziba will split the land between you
p: The rabbis thought David's split verdict was so unjust that it led to the split of his kingdom.
b: David had given Ziba everything (16:4). Now he gives half back to Mephibosheth, without ruling who told the truth. The Babylonian Talmud records a sharp judgment: when David said "you and Ziba will split the land," a heavenly voice answered, "Rehoboam and Jeroboam will split the kingdom" (Bavli Shabbat 56b). The same passage blames David for accepting slander. Modern readers often see a tired king choosing a political compromise: Ziba had helped him in the crisis, and Saul's grandson still had to be watched.

a: He can even take the whole thing
t: Claude's theory: the one who gives up the whole
p: My suggestion: Mephibosheth answers like the true mother before Solomon, who gives up all rather than split it.
b: This is my own reading, labeled as such. In 1 Kings 3:16–28 Solomon orders a baby split in two, and the real mother proves herself by giving up her claim to save the child. Here David orders a field split, and Mephibosheth answers, "He can even take the whole thing," because the king is home safe. The parallel would invite readers to judge Mephibosheth the honest party, as the narrator's note about his mourning (19:24) already hints. I do not know of a commentary that draws this link, though it is simple enough that others have likely seen it. Against it: the scenes are in different books and the verbs differ.

a: Barzillai of Gilead
p: A rich old landowner east of the Jordan who fed David's army at Mahanaim.
b: Barzillai, with Shobi of Ammon and Makir of Lo-debar, brought beds, bowls, grain and food to David's exhausted people at Mahanaim (17:27–29). Rogelim, his home, was in Gilead, but its site is not known. David's last instructions ask Solomon to show loyal love to Barzillai's sons (1 Kings 2:7). A priestly family after the exile called itself "sons of Barzillai" because an ancestor married one of his daughters (Ezra 2:61; Nehemiah 7:63).

a: Do I know good from bad anymore?
p: Here the phrase means the pleasures of the senses: old age has dulled them.
b: "Knowing good and bad" can mean moral knowledge (Genesis 2:17), adult judgment that small children lack (Deuteronomy 1:39; Isaiah 7:15–16), or, as here, telling what tastes or sounds good. Barzillai lists taste and hearing in the same breath. Readers often compare the portrait of old age in Ecclesiastes 12:1–7, where the singers are brought low. Barzillai's honesty about his age is the gentlest refusal in the book.

a: here is your servant Kimham
p: Probably Barzillai's son. A place near Bethlehem later bore his name.
b: Barzillai sends Kimham in his place. The text does not say how they are related, but most readers take him as Barzillai's son, since 1 Kings 2:7 speaks of Barzillai's sons eating at Solomon's table. Centuries later, Jeremiah 41:17 mentions "Geruth Kimham near Bethlehem," a lodging place. Many scholars think David gave Kimham land near his own hometown, which kept the name.

a: steal you away
p: The verb "steal" runs through the Absalom story: Absalom "stole the hearts" of Israel.
b: Israel accuses Judah of "stealing" the king, using the same Hebrew verb (ganav) the narrator used for Absalom, who "stole the hearts" of the men of Israel (15:6), and for the troops who "slipped" (literally "stole") into the city (19:3). Jacob "stole the heart" of Laban when he slipped away (Genesis 31:20, 31:26). The repeated word suggests that the kingdom is still being snatched back and forth, now between tribes.

a: Ten shares in the king belong to us
p: The north counts itself ten tribes against Judah, the same split that will divide the kingdom later.
b: The "ten shares" are the northern tribes, set against Judah (with Simeon, which lived inside Judah). When Solomon's kingdom splits, the prophet Ahijah gives Jeroboam ten pieces of a torn cloak, "ten tribes" (1 Kings 11:30–31). The quarrel here moves straight into Sheba's cry, "We have no share in David" (20:1), which the north repeats word for word when it breaks away from Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:16). The narrator ends the chapter on Judah's harsher words, not on any reconciliation.

a: A worthless man
p: The Hebrew calls Sheba a man of beliya'al, "worthlessness." Later Jewish writings made Belial a name for Satan.
b: Beliya'al probably means "without worth" or "no good," though some scholars connect it with the underworld (see 22:5). A "man" or "son of belial" is a scoundrel who wrecks the community: Eli's sons (1 Samuel 2:12), the men who sneered at Saul (1 Samuel 10:27), Nabal (1 Samuel 25:25). Shimei called David the same thing, "worthless man" (16:7); this site renders the word "worthless" throughout. In the Dead Sea Scrolls Belial is the leader of the forces of darkness, and Paul uses the name for the devil (2 Corinthians 6:15).

a: We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse!
p: Sheba's slogan comes back word for word when the ten northern tribes leave Rehoboam.
b: When Rehoboam refuses to lighten the forced labor, Israel answers with almost the same words: "What share do we have in David? No inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, Israel!" (1 Kings 12:16; 2 Chronicles 10:16). Calling David "the son of Jesse" instead of "the king" is a put-down, as when Saul sneered at him (1 Samuel 20:27, 22:7) and Nabal asked, "Who is the son of Jesse?" (1 Samuel 25:10). Many historians see Sheba's revolt as the first open sign that the union of Judah and Israel under David was fragile.

a: widows for life
p: David shuts away the women Absalom took in public. They live as "widows" while their husband lives.
b: David had left ten concubines to keep the palace (15:16), and Absalom, on Ahithophel's advice, had slept with them in public to show he had taken his father's place (16:21–22), as Nathan had warned (12:11). David now provides for them but never goes to them again. The Hebrew phrase, "widowhood of life," probably means "widows while their husband was alive." Ancient readers took it as necessary: a king could not take back women his son had claimed (compare Reuben, Genesis 35:22 and 49:4). Many modern readers point out that the women suffered twice for the acts of men, and that the narrator gives them no voice.

a: Call out the men of Judah to me
p: David's new commander is told to muster Judah's army in three days. He fails to meet the deadline.
b: Amasa had led Absalom's army against David (17:25); now he is to raise Judah for David. The text does not say why he was late. Judah may have been slow to answer a former rebel; Amasa may simply have lacked Joab's grip on the army. Some readers suspect worse, but the narrator does not hint at treachery. The delay hands the initiative back to Joab's men and his brother Abishai (20:6–7), and it costs Amasa his life.

a: slip out of our sight
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean "escape from our sight" or "do us great harm."
b: Literally the clause is "and snatch away our eye." Most translations take it to mean that Sheba would get away from us, slipping out of view behind town walls. Others read "pluck out our eye," an image of serious harm. Some ancient translators read a different verb meaning "cast a shadow over." The overall sense is clear: if Sheba reaches a walled town, he will be much harder to stop.

a: the great stone in Gibeon
p: A landmark at Gibeon, the town north of Jerusalem where Joab's and Abner's men fought at the pool (2:12–17).
b: Gibeon is el-Jib, about six miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem. Excavations there found a great rock-cut pool and jar handles stamped with the town's name. Joab has history here: at the pool of Gibeon, young men of Joab's and Abner's armies fought, and Abner killed Joab's brother Asahel (2:12–23). Joab later murdered Abner in revenge (3:27). Now he kills Amasa near the same spot. The town also stands behind the story of chapter 21, where Saul's crime against the Gibeonites brings a famine.

a: As he stepped forward, it fell out
p: Did Joab's sword slip by accident or by design? Ancient and modern readers think it was a trick.
b: The Hebrew is hard to follow, but the picture seems to be this: Joab wore his sword in a sheath over his tunic, and as he came forward it dropped out. Josephus, retelling the story, says Joab let it fall on purpose and picked it up as if by chance, so that Amasa saw nothing threatening. Some modern scholars think he had a second short blade in his left hand, as Ehud did (Judges 3:15–22). Either way, Amasa "did not watch out for the sword in Joab's hand" (20:10).

a: took hold of Amasa's beard to kiss him
p: A greeting kiss hides a murder. Joab killed Abner the same way, by a friendly word.
b: Grasping the beard to kiss someone was a warm greeting, and "Are you well, my brother?" (literally "Is it peace?") a friendly question. Joab had already lured Abner aside "to speak with him quietly" and stabbed him in the belly (3:27). David's last words to Solomon name both murders: in time of peace Joab "spilled blood as if at war" (1 Kings 2:5). Proverbs warns that "kisses from someone who hates you come thick and fast" (Proverbs 27:6), and Christian readers have long compared Judas, who greeted Jesus with a kiss to betray him (Matthew 26:49; Luke 22:48).

a: He did not need to strike him again
p: The Hebrew says "he did not repeat to him," a soldier's phrase for a killing blow.
b: Abishai used the same idiom when he offered to kill Saul with one thrust: "I won't have to do it again" (1 Samuel 26:8). The brothers' style is the same. The narrator describes the wound plainly, then moves on at once: Joab and Abishai keep after Sheba as if nothing had happened.

a: after Joab!
p: Joab's young man joins loyalty to David with following Joab, and the troops go along.
b: With Amasa dead, the army needs a leader at once, and one of Joab's men supplies the slogan: whoever is for Joab and whoever is for David, follow Joab. The two are made one. When the campaign ends, the official list names Joab over the whole army again (20:23), as if the appointment of Amasa had never happened. David does not punish Joab now; he leaves it to Solomon (1 Kings 2:5–6, 2:28–34).

a: threw a cloak over him
p: The soldiers stopped at the sight of their dead commander, so the body was hidden from view.
b: Amasa had been named commander by the king (19:13). His body on the road was a shock that could have stopped the pursuit or turned the troops against Joab. Moving the body into a field and covering it got the army moving again. The scene is told from a soldier's eye, without comment.

a: All the Berites
p: No such group is known. Many scholars change one letter and read "the Bichrites," Sheba's own clan.
b: The Hebrew habberim is not explained anywhere else. Several emendations have been proposed: "the Bichrites" (the clan of Bichri, Sheba's father), which fits the story and is followed by some modern translations; "the chosen men" (habbachurim), which seems to lie behind the Latin Vulgate; or the people of Beeroth or Beer. None has manuscript support strong enough to settle the matter, so this translation keeps the Hebrew and notes the problem.

a: Abel of Beth-maacah
p: A large town in the far north, near Dan, now being excavated at Tel Abel Beth Maacah.
b: The site is Tel Abil el-Qameh, a large mound in the Huleh Valley a few miles west of Dan, close to today's border with Lebanon. Excavations led by Nava Panitz-Cohen, Robert Mullins and Naama Yahalom-Mack have uncovered remains from the Iron Age town. It lay on the main road north, on the edge of the Aramean kingdom of Maacah (10:6). Later it was taken by Ben-hadad of Aram (1 Kings 15:20) and by Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Sheba fled about as far north as Israel reached.

a: They heaped up a ramp against the town
p: Attackers piled earth and stones into a ramp to bring battering rams up to a wall.
b: A siege ramp let soldiers reach the upper wall or bring a ram against it. The best-known ancient example is the Assyrian ramp at Lachish (701 BC), still visible, with the Judahite counter-ramp inside. Deuteronomy 20:19–20 sets rules for siege works. Here the ramp "stood level with the outer wall" (Hebrew chel, an outer rampart), and Joab's men were already battering the main wall when the wise woman called out.

a: a wise woman
p: A woman negotiates with Joab and saves her town. She is the second "wise woman" in the David story.
b: Like the wise woman of Tekoa (14:2–20), this woman speaks in proverbs and wins her point with a powerful man. Claudia Camp has argued that such women held a recognized role as counselors in early Israelite towns. She calls her town "a mother in Israel," the title given to Deborah (Judges 5:7), and she persuades her own people to act (20:22). Feminist and literary readers admire her as a peacemaker; others note the price of peace: one man's head. Jewish interpreters identified her with Serah daughter of Asher (Genesis Rabbah 94:9), a legend that made her very old and very wise.

a: a mother in Israel
p: A main town with villages around it was its "mother"; the villages were its "daughters."
b: Hebrew speaks of a town's dependent villages as its "daughters" (Numbers 21:25; Joshua 15:45), so a leading town is a "mother." The word also carries feeling: to destroy a mother town is to strike at Israel's family. Deborah calls herself "a mother in Israel" (Judges 5:7). The woman also calls the town part of "the LORD's inheritance," Israel and its land as God's own property (1 Samuel 26:19).
orig: עִיר וְאֵם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל ('ir ve'em beYisra'el), "a city and a mother in Israel"

a: his head is going to be thrown out to you over the wall
p: Jewish law later debated when a town may hand one person over to save itself, using Sheba as the test case.
b: The rabbis asked: if enemies demand one person from a group on pain of killing all, may the group hand someone over? The Tosefta (Terumot 7:20) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Terumot, chapter 8) answer from this story, but the Yerushalmi records a dispute. Resh Lakish says the person may be handed over only if, like Sheba son of Bichri, he is already liable to death; Rabbi Yochanan says it is enough that the enemy names him. If no one is named, all must refuse. Maimonides rules that a named person may be handed over, but adds that even then "we do not instruct them so" at the outset (Foundations of the Torah 5:5). Christian readers have compared Caiaphas's reasoning that one man should die for the people (John 11:50).

a: Joab was over the whole army of Israel
p: A second list of David's officials, close to the one in 8:16–18, ends the story of the revolts.
b: The list in 8:16–18 closes the account of David's rise and wars; this one closes the long story of David's family troubles (chapters 9–20). The two lists differ: this one adds Adoram over forced labor and Ira the Jairite as David's priest, and it drops the note that David's sons were priests (8:18). Many scholars think the second list reflects the later part of David's reign, when a larger state needed forced labor for building. Some see it as part of a framework that sets chapters 9–20 apart as a "Court History."

a: Adoram was over the forced labor
p: Israel's kings drafted their own people for building. The man in charge of it was later stoned by the north.
b: The Hebrew mas is labor owed to the king, a work draft rather than chattel slavery. Samuel warned that a king would take the people's sons and daughters for his projects (1 Samuel 8:11–17). Under Solomon the draft grew huge (1 Kings 5:13–14), and "Adoniram" (the same man, or a relative) is over it (1 Kings 4:6). When the northern tribes broke away, Rehoboam sent Adoram to them, and they stoned him to death (1 Kings 12:18).

a: Sheva was the scribe
p: The royal scribe has a different name in each list: Seraiah, Sheva (written Sheya), Shisha, Shavsha.
b: The written Hebrew text (the Ketiv) has "Sheya"; the scribes' reading (the Qere) is "Sheva." In 8:17 the scribe is Seraiah, in 1 Chronicles 18:16 Shavsha, and in 1 Kings 4:3 Solomon's scribes are "sons of Shisha." Many scholars think these are forms of one name, possibly not Hebrew. Some suggest it reflects an Egyptian title for a royal letter-writer, since Israel's early court may have copied Egyptian offices. The question is open.

a: Ira the Jairite was David's priest
t: A priest who was not a Levite?
p: Ira came from a clan of Manasseh, not from Levi. What kind of "priest" he was is debated.
b: The Jairites were a clan of Manasseh east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:41). The Hebrew calls Ira a kohen, the normal word for priest, just as 8:18 calls David's sons priests. Some readers think David had personal chaplains or royal priests outside the Levite line, perhaps like the king-priests of the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4). The Targum and some later Jewish interpreters read the word as "chief" or "minister," and 1 Chronicles 18:17 calls David's sons "first in rank beside the king." The question shows how flexible the priesthood seems to have been before the temple.

a: In David's days there was a famine for three years running
p: Chapters 21–24 are an appendix. This story probably comes from early in David's reign, before chapter 9.
b: The last four chapters of the book are not in time order. They gather stories, lists and poems from across David's reign into a careful pattern (see the chapter page). This famine story seems to come early. David spares Mephibosheth (21:7), who first appears in chapter 9, and when Shimei curses David as a man of blood from the house of Saul (16:7–8), he may be thinking of these seven deaths. Rabbinic chronology also put the famine early. Placing it here lets the book end its account of David with two national disasters, both caused by a king, both ended when God accepts prayer for the land (21:14; 24:25).

a: his house of bloodshed
p: Innocent blood not answered for pollutes the land. The famine is the land's sickness.
b: The Hebrew says "the house of bloods," meaning a house guilty of killing. The law teaches that "Blood pollutes the land. No atonement can be made for the land for the blood shed on it, except by the blood of the one who shed it" (Numbers 35:33). Cain's brother's blood cried from the ground and the ground withheld its strength (Genesis 4:10–12). In this view the famine is not random: the land itself refuses to give food while a killing goes unanswered.
orig: בֵּית הַדָּמִים (beit haddamim), "the house of bloods"

a: the Israelites had sworn an oath to them
p: Israel had sworn by the LORD to let the Gibeonites live (Joshua 9). Saul broke the oath.
b: The Gibeonites tricked Joshua into a treaty by pretending to come from far away, and Israel's leaders swore by the LORD to let them live (Joshua 9:15, 9:19–20). Even when the trick came out, the oath held, and the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the sanctuary (Joshua 9:21–27). Saul's attack on them is not told anywhere else. Some connect it with the killing of the priests at Nob (1 Samuel 22:18–19), since the Gibeonites served the sanctuary; others with Beeroth, a Gibeonite town whose people fled (4:2–3).

a: burning with zeal for Israel and Judah
p: Saul attacked the Gibeonites out of zeal for Israel. Here zeal is not praised but condemned.
b: Zeal (qin'ah) can be praised in the Bible, as when Phinehas acts for God's honor (Numbers 25:11–13) or Jehu for the LORD (2 Kings 10:16). Saul's zeal looks like nationalism: he wanted the land for Israel and Judah alone. But Israel had sworn to protect these people, and God holds Israel to the oath even generations later. Some readers see Saul trying to finish Joshua's conquest; others connect the zeal with his violence against Nob (1 Samuel 22). Either way, a promise made in God's name to foreigners outweighed a king's patriotic cause.

a: with what shall I make atonement?
p: Kipper here means to wipe out a wrong by paying for it, so that the wronged party can bless instead of curse.
b: The verb kipper is the word of the sacrificial laws, "make atonement." Its root idea seems to be to wipe clean or to pay a ransom (kofer). David asks what payment will settle the wrong, so that the Gibeonites will bless Israel instead of cursing it. But the law did not allow a ransom for murder: "Do not take a ransom for the life of a murderer who is guilty and deserves to die" (Numbers 35:31). The Gibeonites know this, and refuse silver and gold (21:4).

a: Nor are we free to kill anyone in Israel
p: As non-Israelites under Israel's protection, the Gibeonites had no right to take blood vengeance themselves.
b: The Gibeonites lived among Israel as protected outsiders. They could not avenge their dead the way an Israelite family could through its "avenger of blood" (Numbers 35:19). Their answer is careful and polite: they do not want money, and they will not act on their own. They wait for the king to ask what they want, and only then name their price (21:6). In the ancient Near East a broken treaty sworn by the gods was thought to bring plague or famine until it was made good. The Hittite king Mursili II prayed in the 1300s BC about a plague he blamed on his father's breach of a treaty oath.

a: We will impale them before the LORD
p: The rare verb hoqia' describes a form of execution and display. Its exact meaning is uncertain.
b: The same verb is used when Moses is told to "impale" the leaders of the people "before the LORD in the open sun" after the sin at Baal-peor (Numbers 25:4). Ancient and modern translators have offered "hang," "crucify," "impale," "expose" and "break the limbs" (from a related verb used of Jacob's hip being put out of joint, Genesis 32:25). What is clear is that the bodies were left out in public "before the LORD" as a sign of covenant punishment. This translation uses "impale," as the site does at Numbers 25:4, and leaves the details alone.

a: the LORD's chosen one
p: Saul is called "chosen" by the LORD. Some think the words are a bitter jab; others think the text is damaged.
b: Saul was the man "the LORD has chosen" (1 Samuel 10:24), and the Gibeonites may use the title with irony: they will execute the chosen king's sons in his own town. Some scholars think the words were miscopied and once read "on the mountain of the LORD," which would match 21:9 ("on the hill before the LORD"). The Greek (Vaticanus, the kaige text, and the Lucianic manuscripts alike, as reported) also has "the chosen of the Lord" here, so the change would have happened early if it happened at all. The Greek also places the deed "in Gibeon" rather than "in Gibeah"; see the variant.

a: because of the oath of the LORD between them
t: David keeps his oath to Jonathan
p: David spares Jonathan's son because of the friends' sworn covenant.
b: Jonathan had asked David to swear never to cut off his loyal love from Jonathan's house (1 Samuel 20:14–17, 20:42), and David had already shown that loyalty by bringing Mephibosheth to his table (9:1–13). Now one oath (Israel's to the Gibeonites) demands Saulide lives, and another (David's to Jonathan) protects one of them. The story weighs oaths heavily on both sides. A second Mephibosheth, Saul's son by Rizpah, is not spared (21:8).

a: Rizpah daughter of Aiah
p: Saul's concubine, mother of two of his sons. Abner's affair with her once split Saul's house (3:7).
b: Rizpah first appears when Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with her, a claim to Saul's throne, and Abner angrily goes over to David (3:6–11). Now her two sons by Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, are handed to the Gibeonites. She says nothing in the story; her actions speak (21:10).

a: they impaled them on the hill before the LORD
p: Seven of Saul's descendants die for Saul's crime. Readers have read the story in three main ways.
b: Justice for a broken oath. Many Jewish and Christian readers see a hard but real justice: Saul broke an oath sworn in God's name, his house shared his guilt ("his house of bloodshed," 21:1), and the oath had to be honored. The narrator has God himself name the cause (21:1). The Talmud discusses this case directly, including why the bodies were left out despite Deuteronomy 21:23, and teaches that it is better to uproot a letter of the Torah than to profane God's name in public (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a). A political purge. Critical scholars such as McCarter, Halpern and McKenzie note that the deaths removed nearly all of Saul's male heirs and suited David well, and that David himself chose which descendants would die (21:7–8); Shimei's charge in 16:7–8 may reflect such suspicion. A theological problem. The law forbids putting children to death for their fathers' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), and some readers note that God's acceptance of prayer is reported only after the bones are buried (21:14). Others answer that the rain of 21:10, the sign that the drought was ending, fell while the bodies still hung, so the text may not separate the two so sharply. See the chapter page.

a: when the barley harvest began
p: Barley was the first grain harvested, in April, around Passover.
b: In the land of Israel barley ripens first, in March or April, and wheat a few weeks later. Ruth and Naomi reached Bethlehem "at the beginning of the barley harvest" (Ruth 1:22). The seven men died at the very season when a famine-struck land hoped for food. If the rain of 21:10 was the autumn rain (October or November), Rizpah's watch lasted about half a year. Some readers think an out-of-season rain is meant, a sign that the drought had ended.

a: Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth
p: A grieving mother guards the bodies for months. Her silent protest moves David to give Saul's family a burial.
b: Leaving bodies to birds and beasts was the worst disgrace in the ancient world (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Samuel 17:44), and the law said an executed man must be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Rizpah cannot stop the executions, but she will not let the bodies be eaten. Sackcloth was the coarse cloth of mourning. Her watch, day and night, is the turning point: when David hears of it, he gathers the bones and buries them with Saul and Jonathan (21:11–14). Many readers find in her one of the Bible's great portraits of a mother's love and of protest without words.

a: stretched it out on the rock
p: Greek tragedy has a woman who defies a king to bury her brother. Is there a link?
b: In Sophocles' play Antigone (about 441 BC), a king forbids burial of a rebel, and his niece Antigone buries her brother anyway and dies for it. Readers have often set her beside Rizpah: both are women who honor the dead against the orders of the powerful. The verdict: there is no literary link. The stories are centuries and cultures apart. What they share is the common ancient belief that leaving the dead unburied was a horror, and a common moral picture of a woman's loyalty facing royal power.

a: the men of Jabesh-gilead
p: The men of Jabesh had rescued Saul's body from the wall of Beth-shan at great risk.
b: Saul had rescued Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite (1 Samuel 11). After the battle of Gilboa, when the Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan, the men of Jabesh marched all night, took down the bodies, burned them and buried the bones (1 Samuel 31:11–13). David had thanked them for it (2:4–7). Now David moves the bones to the family tomb, completing the honor Jabesh began.

a: in the tomb of his father Kish
p: To be buried in the family tomb was to be "gathered to one's fathers." David gives Saul his proper rest.
b: Zela was a town of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28); its site is not known. Israelite families buried their dead in rock-cut tombs used for generations, with bones gathered into a side chamber to make room. Burying Saul, Jonathan and the seven executed men together in Kish's tomb gives Saul's house honor and peace. It also answers any charge that David had treated Saul's family with contempt.

a: God accepted the prayers made for the land
p: The same phrase ends chapter 24. In both stories the land's disaster ends when God hears prayer.
b: The Hebrew verb ne'tar means "to let oneself be entreated," to accept a plea. It ends this famine story and the plague story at the end of the book (24:25), forming a frame around the appendix. Notice where it comes: not after the executions (21:9) but after the bones are buried (21:14). Some readers, such as Walter Brueggemann, see the narrator's quiet point here: God did not need the blood of the seven; what moved things was Rizpah's devotion and David's act of honor.

a: David was worn out
p: David tires in battle and nearly dies. His men decide he must not fight anymore.
b: The four giant stories (21:15–22) probably come from the wars with the Philistines early in David's reign (5:17–25), but the first one shows David weak. It may explain why David stayed home from war in later years (11:1; 18:3). The note fits the appendix's portrait of a king whose strength is not his own: in the next chapter he will sing that God trains his hands for battle (22:35).

a: born to the Rapha
p: A name tied to the Rephaim, the giants of old. It may name a family, an ancestor, or a warrior band.
b: The phrase "born to the Rapha" (or "descendants of the Rapha") describes all four Philistine champions here (21:16, 21:18, 21:20, 21:22). Most readers connect it with the Rephaim, the tall ancient peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:11, 2:20; 3:11). The Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem keeps the name (5:18; 23:13). Some scholars, such as Folker Willesen, suggested instead a warrior guild dedicated to a god or hero called Rapha, since "born to" can mean members of a group. Texts from Ugarit speak of the rapi'uma, honored dead heroes. The question is open.

a: he was armed with new gear
p: The Hebrew says only that he was girded with "new" (feminine). The noun is missing.
b: Most translations supply "a new sword," since a sword is girded on. Others think of new armor, or suspect a copying error. The weight of his spear (the word may mean the spearhead), three hundred shekels of bronze (about 7.5 pounds, 3.4 kg), is half that of Goliath's iron spearhead (1 Samuel 17:7).

a: Do not snuff out Israel's lamp
p: A lamp stands for life and for a family line that goes on. David is Israel's lamp.
b: In a dark house a burning lamp meant someone was alive inside. So a lamp became a picture of a family's survival: God promises that David will always have "a lamp" in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19), and Psalm 132:17 speaks of "a lamp for my anointed." David's men call him the lamp of the whole nation. In the next chapter David sings, "My lamp is you, LORD" (22:29): the king who is Israel's lamp has his own light from God.

a: Sibbecai the Hushathite
p: One of David's warriors, later commander of a monthly division of the army.
b: Sibbecai appears in the Chronicler's list of David's warriors (1 Chronicles 11:29) and as commander for the eighth month (1 Chronicles 27:11). In the list in 23:27 the name "Mebunnai" stands in his place, probably by a copying error, since the Hebrew letters are similar. Gob is unknown; 1 Chronicles 20:4 places this battle at Gezer.

a: Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite
p: 1 Samuel 17 says David killed Goliath; this verse says Elhanan; 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Goliath's brother.
b: In 1 Samuel 17 the champion is "a champion named Goliath, from Gath" (1 Samuel 17:4), and "His spear had a shaft like the beam on a weavers' loom" (1 Samuel 17:7), the same comparison used here. The answers (see the note on 1 Samuel 17:4 and the variants here): (1) Chronicles kept the better text, "Lahmi the brother of Goliath," and Samuel's copy was damaged; "Lahmi" and "the Bethlehemite" look alike in Hebrew. (2) Elhanan is another name for David (the Targum, Rashi). (3) There were two men named Goliath. (4) Many critical scholars think Elhanan's deed was later told of David. The odd name "Jaare-oregim" seems to have picked up "oregim" ("weavers") from the end of the verse.

a: came six to each
p: Extra fingers and toes (polydactyly) is a real inherited trait, so the detail fits a family of warriors.
b: Having extra fingers or toes is a known inherited condition and often runs in families. The note fits the phrase "born to the Rapha": a family marked by great height and this unusual trait. Ancient readers loved such details, and 1 Chronicles 20:6 repeats it.

a: Jonathan son of Shimeah, David's brother
p: Shimeah is David's brother, also called Shammah. His other son was the clever Jonadab.
b: Jesse's third son is called Shammah (1 Samuel 16:9; 17:13), Shimeah (13:3; here), and Shimea (1 Chronicles 2:13). The written Hebrew here has "Shimei." His son Jonadab gave Amnon the advice that led to the rape of Tamar (13:3–5, 13:32–33). Another son, Jonathan, kills this giant who jeers at Israel, as David did the first giant who defied Israel's ranks (1 Samuel 17:10, 17:26).

a: David and his servants brought them down
p: David killed none of these four. The summary credits the king with what his men did.
b: Hebrew can say a king did what his army did. Some readers count Goliath (1 Samuel 17) as one of the four, so that David's own giant is included, but the list here has four other names (Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath of 21:19, and the six-fingered man). The point of the summary is that the old terror of the giants, which had frightened Israel since the spies (Numbers 13:33), ended under David.

a: These are the words of the song David spoke to the LORD
p: This song appears again in the Bible as Psalm 18, with many small differences.
b: Psalm 18 opens with almost the same heading, adding "For the music director. Of the LORD's servant, David." The two copies agree in most lines but differ in dozens of small places, in spelling, word choice and line length. They are two copies of one poem that were handed down separately, one in the book of Samuel and one in the temple's hymnbook. The opening words echo Moses, who "spoke the words of this song" before Israel (Deuteronomy 31:30), so David's song at the end of his story stands where Moses' song stands at the end of his. The chapter page lists the main differences between the two copies.

a: from the grip of all his enemies and from the grip of Saul
p: The heading ties it to David's rescue from his enemies. Scholars date it from David's day to the later kings.
b: The heading sets the song after David's wars were won (compare 7:1, "the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies"). Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman argued from its old spelling and grammar that the poem is very ancient, perhaps from the 900s BC, close to David's own time. Others think it is a royal hymn written for later kings of David's line and credited to him. Its place near the end of the book, not after chapter 8 or chapter 10, is a choice of the book's editors: David's praise comes after his sins and his sorrows, not only after his victories.

a: He said:
p: Psalm 18 begins "I love you, LORD, my strength." The Samuel copy lacks this line.
b: Psalm 18:1 has a line the Samuel copy does not: "I love you, LORD, my strength." The verb (racham, usually "show compassion") is used for loving God only here in the Bible, and many scholars think the line was added when the song entered the temple's worship. Samuel's copy starts straight with the list of names for God. The two copies are numbered differently: 2 Samuel 22:2–3 together match Psalm 18:2, so from 22:4 on each verse of Samuel is one number higher than its match in the Psalm (22:4 is Psalm 18:3).
orig: Psalm 18:1 אֶרְחָמְךָ יְהוָה חִזְקִי (erchamkha YHWH chizqi)

a: The LORD is my high cliff, my fortress
p: David's names for God come from the places where he hid from Saul.
b: The Hebrew sela' is a high cliff or crag, and metsudah is a mountain stronghold, the word for David's hideouts in the wilderness (1 Samuel 22:4–5; 24:22). Saul once chased David around a mountain at a spot named "the Rock of Escape" (Sela' hammachleqot, 1 Samuel 23:28). In 22:3 the word changes to tsur, a rock or boulder, the word Moses used: "He is the Rock" (Deuteronomy 32:4). The song gathers David's memories of the wilderness into names for God.

a: the horn that saves me
p: A horn stands for strength, like the horns of a wild ox. "Horn of salvation" means strong rescuer.
b: In the Bible an animal's horn is a picture of power: "my horn is lifted high" means "I am made strong." Hannah's song opens and closes with the horn: "my horn is raised high by the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:1), and God will "raise high his anointed one's horn" (1 Samuel 2:10). David's song uses the same picture near the end of the same book. Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, takes up the phrase when he praises God for raising up "a horn of salvation" in the house of David (Luke 1:69).
r: 1 Samuel 2:1; 1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 18:2; Psalm 89:17; Psalm 132:17; Luke 1:69

a: Death's breakers swept around me
p: Samuel has "breakers of death"; Psalm 18:4 has "cords of death." Drowning and trapping both follow.
b: Samuel's mishberei mavet are breaking waves, the word Jonah uses: "all your breakers and your waves passed over me" (Jonah 2:3). Psalm 18:4 has chevlei mavet, "cords of death," which matches the ropes and snares in the next line (22:6). Either could be original. The "floods of ruin" are literally "torrents of beliya'al," the word used of worthless men (20:1; 23:6); here it seems to mean destruction or the underworld itself.

a: The ropes of Sheol
p: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the world of the dead, here pictured as a hunter with ropes and snares.
b: Sheol is where all the dead go, deep beneath the earth (Genesis 37:35; 1 Samuel 2:6). Here it is pictured as a hunter laying ropes and traps, and as deep waters (22:5). David means that he came to the edge of death, not that he died. Readers who take the song as a prayer of Jesus, or of every believer, have heard in these lines a picture of being rescued from death itself.

a: He heard my voice in his temple
p: The temple was not built until Solomon. The "temple" here is God's palace in heaven.
b: The Hebrew heikhal means a palace or a temple. Since Solomon's temple did not exist yet, most readers take it as God's heavenly palace, from which he comes down in the next lines (22:10). The tent shrine at Shiloh was also called a heikhal (1 Samuel 1:9; 3:3). Psalm 18:6 has a longer last line: "my cry for help came before him, into his ears."

a: the base of the heavens shuddered
p: Samuel says the base of the heavens shook; Psalm 18:7 says the base of the mountains.
b: Ancient Israelites pictured the sky as a dome resting on the mountains or on pillars at the edge of the earth (Job 26:11). So "the base of the heavens" and "the base of the mountains" may be two ways of naming the same place. See the variant on this phrase.

a: Up went smoke from his nose
p: The LORD comes in smoke, fire, thunder and darkness. Canaanite poems describe the storm god Baal the same way.
b: The pictures of 22:8–16 belong to an old poetic tradition of the storm god's coming: the earth shakes, the god thunders, rides the clouds and shoots lightning arrows. Texts from Ugarit (1300s–1200s BC) give Baal the title "Rider of the Clouds" and describe his voice as thunder. Israel's poets use the same language for the LORD (Psalm 29; Psalm 68:4; Habakkuk 3), and the Sinai story has smoke, fire and quaking (Exodus 19:16–18). The verdict: the shared imagery is real, but the song makes a pointed claim. The LORD, not Baal, rules the storm, and he comes down to rescue one man.

a: Riding a cherub, he flew
p: God rides a cherub as a chariot, as he is "enthroned on the cherubim" above the ark.
b: Cherubim were winged creatures that guarded holy places (Genesis 3:24) and spread their wings over the ark (Exodus 25:18–22). God is called the one "enthroned on the cherubim" (6:2; 1 Samuel 4:4). In Ezekiel's vision, living creatures with wings carry God's throne-chariot (Ezekiel 1; 10). Here the cherub is God's steed in the storm, and the wind has "wings." See the variant on "came into view."

a: the Most High
p: Elyon, "Most High," is an old title for God, first used for the God of Melchizedek.
b: Elyon is used of "God Most High" whose priest was Melchizedek of Salem (Genesis 14:18–22), and of the God who divided the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8). It is common in the Psalms. Here it stands in parallel with "the LORD": the thunder of the storm is his voice.

a: The sea's channels showed
p: The LORD's breath uncovers the sea's floor, as at the crossing of the sea.
b: Moses' song says, "By the wind from your nostrils / the waters were heaped up" (Exodus 15:8). David's song uses the same picture: at the blast of God's breath the sea bed shows. The rescue of one king is told in the language of the exodus, and of creation, when God set boundaries for the waters (Psalm 104:6–9). Psalm 18:15 addresses God directly here: "at your rebuke, LORD."

a: he pulled me from great waters
p: The verb mashah, "draw out," is the verb behind the name Moses.
b: Mashah is used only three times in the Bible: here, in Psalm 18:16, and when Pharaoh's daughter names the baby Moses: "From the water I drew him" (Exodus 2:10). David, rescued from "great waters," is drawn out like Moses. "Great waters" (mayim rabbim) is a common picture of chaos and of enemy nations (Psalm 144:7; Isaiah 17:12–13).

a: The LORD treated me as my righteousness deserved
t: How can David claim to be righteous?
p: After Bathsheba and Uriah, David's claim of clean hands sounds strange. Readers explain it in several ways.
b: David sings that God rewarded his righteousness and clean hands (22:21–25). Yet the reader has just read of adultery and murder (chapters 11–12). Explanations: (1) The song comes from early in David's reign, before his great sin, as the heading's mention of Saul suggests. (2) David claims innocence in his conflict with Saul, not a sinless life; he never raised his hand against the LORD's anointed. (3) "Righteousness" here means loyalty to the covenant and its God, which a repentant sinner can still claim, not perfection (compare Psalm 51). (4) Many critical scholars see a royal hymn whose king is the ideal king, not David as he was. Christian readers have often heard the words fully true only of the Messiah.

a: All his rulings stand before me
p: Two words for God's law, mishpatim and chuqqot, the pair Deuteronomy uses.
b: The pair is Deuteronomy's own: God's "rules" (chuqqim, here the feminine chuqqot) and "rulings" (mishpatim), as this site translates them throughout. The king who sings it keeps the law the way Deuteronomy's law of the king asks: he is to read it all his life and not turn aside from the command (Deuteronomy 17:18–20).

a: With him I have been wholehearted
p: The key word tamim, "whole, complete, blameless," comes four times in a few lines, for David and for God.
b: Tamim is used of sacrificial animals without defect ("flawless") and of people who are whole in their devotion. This site translates it "wholehearted" or "blameless" for people and "flawless" for animals. The song repeats it: David has been wholehearted with God (22:24); God is wholehearted with the wholehearted (22:26); God's way is flawless (22:31); and God makes David's way whole (22:33). The repetition makes the point that David's integrity reflects God's own.

a: With the loyal you show yourself loyal
p: God deals with each kind of person in that person's own way, even outwitting the twisted.
b: The "loyal" (chasid) are people who keep hesed, loyal love, the word in the song's last line (22:51). The verbs in 22:26–27 are reflexive: God "shows himself" loyal, wholehearted, pure. With the crooked he "twists and turns" (Hebrew titappal), meaning he outwits them on their own ground, not that God becomes crooked. Proverbs says something similar: "With mockers he mocks, but to the humble he gives grace" (Proverbs 3:34; compare James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5).

a: My lamp is you, LORD
p: Samuel's copy calls God the lamp; Psalm 18:28 says God lights David's lamp.
b: David's men had called David "Israel's lamp" (21:17). Here David says the LORD himself is his lamp. Psalm 18:28 reads differently: "You light my lamp, LORD; / my God makes my darkness bright." The Psalm has a whole extra verb, ta'ir, "you light," so this is not a one-letter difference; Samuel's line is shorter (ki 'attah neri, "for you are my lamp"). The thought is the same: the king's light comes from God.

a: I rush at a war party
p: The Hebrew gedud is a raiding band. Some read a similar word meaning "wall" or "rampart."
b: Gedud is the word for raiders, such as the Amalekite band David chased (1 Samuel 30:8). With God's help David charges them and leaps over walls. Some scholars, matching the second line, read gader, "wall," and translate "I run through a rampart." The picture is the same either way: no obstacle can stop the king God strengthens.

a: The LORD's word is refined like metal
p: This verse is quoted in Proverbs 30:5. God's word, like refined silver, has no impurity.
b: The verb tsaraf is used of smelting metal to burn away the dross. Psalm 12:6 says, "The LORD's sayings are sayings without impurity, silver smelted in a crucible in the ground, refined seven times." Proverbs 30:5 quotes this line almost exactly: every word of God is refined; he is a shield to those who take shelter in him. The song moves from God's rescue to the trustworthiness of what he says.

a: Who is God, if not the LORD?
p: Hannah asked the same thing at the start of the book: "There is no rock like our God."
b: The question sums up the faith of the whole song. Hannah's song says, "There is no rock like our God" (1 Samuel 2:2), and Moses sings that the nations' rock is not like Israel's Rock (Deuteronomy 32:31). In Isaiah God himself says that there is no god apart from him and no other rock that he knows of (Isaiah 44:8). The books of Samuel open and close with songs that say the same thing.

a: He makes my feet like a doe's
p: Mountain deer climb rocky heights without slipping. Habakkuk borrows the line.
b: Mountain goats and deer in the Judean wilderness move easily on cliffs where people fall. David, who lived in that wilderness, sings that God gives him the same sure footing. Habakkuk ends his book with the same words (Habakkuk 3:19). "My high places" may be battle heights or the land itself, as when Moses says God made Israel ride on the heights of the earth (Deuteronomy 32:13).

a: my arms can draw a bronze bow
p: No working bow was made of solid bronze. The phrase means a very strong bow.
b: Bows in David's time were made of wood or of wood, horn and sinew glued together (the composite bow). Bronze bows were not used in war, though bows might have bronze fittings. Job 20:24 also speaks of a "bronze bow." The picture is of a bow so stiff only great strength could draw it, and God gives that strength. Compare Odysseus' bow in Homer's Odyssey, which no suitor could string.

a: when you answer me, you make me great
p: Samuel reads "your answering"; Psalm 18:35 reads "your gentleness" or "your humility."
b: The two Hebrew words differ by one letter: Samuel's 'anotkha, "your answering," and the Psalm's 'anvatkha, "your humility" or "gentleness." The Psalm's reading is bold: God's stooping down is what makes the king great. Jewish teachers drew a lesson from such verses: wherever Scripture speaks of God's greatness, it also speaks of his humility (Bavli Megillah 31a, citing other verses). Psalm 18:35 also has an extra line: "your right hand holds me up." See the variant.

a: You gave me my enemies' necks
p: To give someone the necks of enemies is to make them turn and run, or to put them under one's foot.
b: The Hebrew says "you gave me my enemies, a neck." The picture is of enemies turning their backs in flight, so that the pursuer sees only their necks (Exodus 23:27), or of a victor setting his foot on the neck of the defeated (Joshua 10:24). Jacob's blessing on Judah says, "Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies" (Genesis 49:8).

a: They looked around, and there was no rescuer
p: Samuel has "they looked"; Psalm 18:41 has "they cried for help." The two verbs look alike.
b: Samuel's yish'u, "they looked," and the Psalm's yeshavve'u, "they cried for help," share most of their letters. The Psalm's reading makes a sharper picture: the enemies cry even to the LORD, and he does not answer. Either way, the enemy's gods and the enemy's prayers fail.

a: you guarded me to be chief over the nations
p: David's empire in chapter 8 lies behind this line. Later readers heard a promise for the Messiah.
b: David ruled or took tribute from Moab, Edom, Ammon and the Aramean kingdoms (8:1–14; 10:19), and foreign kings like Hiram of Tyre sought his friendship (5:11). The song praises God for this. "My own people's feuds" may mean the revolts of Absalom and Sheba (Samuel) or "the strife of the people" in general (Psalm 18:43). Jewish and Christian readers have read the line together with Psalm 2:8, where God gives his king the nations as an inheritance, as a promise that a son of David will rule the world.

a: Sons of foreign lands fawn on me
p: The verb kichesh means to deceive. Here it describes foreigners who pretend loyalty out of fear.
b: Kichesh usually means to lie or deny (Genesis 18:15; Joshua 24:27). Said of defeated enemies, it describes forced, insincere submission, cringing obedience. The same phrase appears in Psalm 66:3 and Psalm 81:15. The foreign kings obey the moment they hear of David, not because they love him but because they fear him.

a: they come limping out of their fortresses
p: Samuel's verb seems to mean "gird themselves" or "limp"; Psalm 18:45 has "come trembling."
b: Samuel's yachgeru normally means "they gird themselves," which makes little sense here; some connect it with an Aramaic word for "limp." Psalm 18:45 has yacheregu, "they come out trembling," with two letters in a different order. Micah 7:17 paints a close picture with a different verb: nations come trembling out of their strongholds. This translation keeps Samuel's word with the sense "limping."

a: The LORD is alive!
p: Usually the start of an oath ("by the life of the LORD"); here it is a shout of praise.
b: "As the LORD lives" is the most common oath in the Bible (for example 1 Samuel 26:10). Here the same words, chai YHWH, stand alone as an acclamation: the LORD is living and active, unlike idols. Some scholars compare the cry of Baal's worshipers in the Ugarit poems when their god returns to life, "Mighty Baal is alive," and see a deliberate contrast: Israel's God never needs to come back from death.

a: That is why I will give you thanks among the nations, LORD
p: Paul quotes this verse (from Psalm 18:49) to show that Gentiles were meant to praise God with Israel.
b: In Romans 15:8–12 Paul strings together Old Testament verses about the nations praising God, and this is the first: "That is why I will confess you among the nations and make music to your name" (Romans 15:9, quoting Psalm 18:49). For Paul, David's praise "among the nations" pointed ahead to a day when the nations themselves would worship Israel's God through the Messiah, David's son.

a: he shows loyal love to his anointed
t: His anointed, David and his line
p: The song ends with God's loyal love for David's line forever, the promise of chapter 7.
b: The last line gathers up God's promise to David: a house, a throne and a kingdom forever, and loyal love that will not be taken away as it was from Saul (7:12–16). "His anointed" (meshicho) is the king, and Hannah's song ended the same way: God will "raise high his anointed one's horn" (1 Samuel 2:10). Jewish tradition reads the line of the Messiah in "David and his line for all time." Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, "son of David" (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32–33). Critical readers note that the line fits a king's thanksgiving sung in the temple for the ruling son of David.

a: These are David's last words
p: Like Jacob and Moses, David leaves last words. 1 Kings 2:1–9 gives a second, very different set.
b: Great leaders in the Bible leave a final poem or charge: Jacob blesses his sons (Genesis 49), Moses blesses the tribes (Deuteronomy 33), Joshua renews the covenant (Joshua 23–24). David's "last words" here are a short prophetic poem about a just king and God's everlasting covenant. They are not his last words in time: in 1 Kings 2:1–9 the dying David gives Solomon practical and sometimes harsh advice about Joab and Shimei. Many readers think the book of Samuel chose to end David's speaking with this poem, his ideal, and left the politics to Kings.

a: The declaration of David son of Jesse
p: The word ne'um usually introduces a prophet's message from God. It frames David's words as prophecy.
b: Ne'um appears hundreds of times in the phrase "declares the LORD." Only rarely is it used of a human speaker, and the closest parallel is Balaam, the seer, who opens his visions by naming himself twice with ne'um and calling himself "the man" whose eye sees true (Numbers 24:3–4, 24:15–16). David's lines follow the same pattern: the declaration of David son of Jesse, the declaration of the man set up on high. A man's words become an oracle because, as the next verse says, the LORD's Spirit speaks through him. See also Proverbs 30:1.

a: the man set up on high
t: "Set up on high" or "whom God raised up"?
p: The Hebrew reads 'al, "on high." Ancient witnesses seem to read 'el, "God": "the man God raised up."
b: The Masoretic Text has huqam 'al, "raised on high." The Greek of Codex Vaticanus (the kaige text) reads something like "whom the Lord raised up," and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a is reported to read heqim 'el, "God raised up" (Ulrich; McCarter). The two readings differ in a consonant ('ayin in 'al, aleph in 'el) and in the form of the verb. Both readings make the same point, that David did not raise himself: God took him from the sheepfold (7:8). Because I could not check the scroll itself in DJD 17, the Plain keeps the Hebrew and the variant on this verse gives the other reading as reported.

a: the darling of Israel's songs
p: The phrase can mean Israel's sweet singer, the favorite of Israel's songs, or the favorite of Israel's Mighty One.
b: Ne'im zemirot Yisra'el is famous from the King James Version's "the sweet psalmist of Israel," which made David the singer of the Psalms. The words can also mean "the one Israel's songs delight in," the hero of songs like "Saul has struck his thousands, / David his tens of thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7). A third reading takes zimrah in its other sense, "strength, protection" (as in Exodus 15:2): "the favorite of the Strong One of Israel." This translation chooses the middle sense, the same option the NIV takes, because it fits the parallel lines about David's status, and notes that the first sense has a long and honored history in Jewish and Christian tradition.

a: The LORD's Spirit has spoken by me
p: David claims that the Spirit spoke through him. The New Testament calls David a prophet on this basis.
b: The Spirit came on David when Samuel anointed him (1 Samuel 16:13). Here David says that the Spirit has put words on his tongue. Jesus introduces a psalm with "David himself, speaking by the Holy Spirit, said" (Mark 12:36), and Peter calls David "a prophet" who foresaw the Messiah (Acts 2:30). Jewish tradition counted the Psalms among the writings composed with the holy spirit. Critical scholars often date this poem later than David, but agree that it presents the king as one who speaks for God.
r: 1 Samuel 16:13; Mark 12:36; Matthew 22:43; Acts 1:16; Acts 2:30; 2 Peter 1:21

a: Someone who rules humankind in righteousness
p: A picture of the ideal king. Jewish and Christian readers alike heard it as a portrait of the Messiah.
b: The oracle describes a ruler who governs with justice and in reverence for God, and compares him to sunrise and rain (23:4). Read in its setting, it is God's ideal for every king of David's line, a standard David himself did not always meet. The Targum of the Prophets reads the passage as speaking of the Messiah who will arise and rule in the fear of the LORD. Christian readers have linked it with the promises of a righteous branch of David (Isaiah 11:1–5; Jeremiah 23:5) fulfilled in Jesus. Critical scholars see a royal ideal like Psalm 72.

a: he is like morning light as the sun rises
p: A just king brings life the way morning sun and rain bring grass out of the ground.
b: Psalm 72, a prayer for the king, uses the same pictures: "May he come down like rain on mown grass" (Psalm 72:6). Hosea compares God's coming to the dawn and the spring rain (Hosea 6:3), and Malachi pictures righteousness rising like the sun, with healing in its rays (Malachi 4:2). In the dry land of Israel, sun after rain meant new grass and a living land.

a: a covenant with me that lasts forever
p: David's last words return to God's promise in chapter 7: a house and a throne forever.
b: Nathan brought God's promise that David's house, kingdom and throne would stand forever (7:12–16). Here David calls that promise a "covenant" (berit), a word chapter 7 does not use. Psalm 89 does: "I have made a covenant with the one I chose" (Psalm 89:3), and Isaiah offers the whole people "an everlasting covenant, my faithful loves for David" (Isaiah 55:3). The first line can be read as a question ("Is my house not like this with God?") or as an admission ("For my house is not so with God"), and translators divide. As a question, it expresses confidence; as a statement, it admits failure and then holds on to the covenant anyway.

a: the worthless are thorns
p: The wicked are like thorns: no one handles them bare-handed, and in the end they are burned.
b: Thorny brush was cleared with tools and burned in heaps (Isaiah 33:12). The picture is the opposite of the grass of 23:4: the righteous ruler makes life grow, while the worthless (Hebrew beliya'al, as in 20:1 and 16:7) are cleared away. Jesus' parable of the weeds burned at the harvest (Matthew 13:30, 13:40–42) and Hebrews 6:8 use similar pictures.

a: on the spot
p: The last word of the poem, bashshevet, is obscure. It may mean "where they lie," or it may be a copying slip.
b: Bashshevet looks like "in the sitting" or "in the dwelling." Many translators take it as "on the spot," "where they lie." Others think it was copied by mistake from the first words of the next verse, "Josheb-basshebeth" (23:8), which share the same letters. The meaning of the line is clear either way: the thorns are burned up.

a: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite
p: "Josheb-basshebeth" means "sitting in the seat." Chronicles has "Jashobeam"; the original may have been "Ishbaal."
b: The name as written is odd, and it may have been changed. 1 Chronicles 11:11 has "Jashobeam son of Hachmoni." Codex Vaticanus (the kaige text) has "Iebosthe" (a form of Ishbosheth), and the Lucianic manuscripts, the better witness to the Old Greek here, have "Iesbaal" (see the variant). Many scholars, including McCarter, think the warrior's name was Ishbaal, "man of the master," and that scribes changed baal to bosheth, "shame," as they did with Saul's son Ish-bosheth (2:8; compare Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles 8:33). "Tahchemonite" seems to be a form of "son of Hachmoni."

a: chief of the Three
p: David's best fighters formed two honored groups: the Three and the Thirty.
b: The list names three top heroes (Josheb-basshebeth, Eleazar, Shammah), then two men who outranked the Thirty but did not reach the Three (Abishai, Benaiah), then the Thirty. The Hebrew word in this verse, hashshalishi, is not a Ketiv and Qere pair; it is one ambiguous form that may mean "the officers" (from the word for a chariot's third man or an officer, Exodus 14:7) rather than "the Three" (see the variant). Chronicles has "the Thirty" or "the officers," depending on the reading followed. Benjamin Mazar argued that the Thirty were an official council of David's elite officers, perhaps on a foreign model; Karl Elliger studied how the list grew. Many of the men came from Bethlehem and nearby Judah, David's early followers.

a: who had massed there for battle
p: The place name seems to have dropped out. Chronicles names it: Pas-dammim.
b: "There" has nothing to refer to in Samuel's text. The parallel, 1 Chronicles 11:13, says Eleazar was with David "at Pas-dammim," probably Ephes-dammim, where the Philistines camped before Goliath's challenge (1 Samuel 17:1). Most scholars think the name was lost in copying. Chronicles also blends Eleazar's stand with the next story (Shammah's field), so its account is shorter.

a: son of Ahohi
t: Son of Ahohi, or the Ahohite?
p: The Hebrew says "son of Ahohi." Chronicles and 23:28 have "the Ahohite," a clan name.
b: The Masoretic Text reads ben-'Achochi, "son of Ahohi." 1 Chronicles 11:12 has "Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite," and 23:28 in this list names "Zalmon the Ahohite." Ahoah was a Benjaminite clan (1 Chronicles 8:4). Many translations read "the Ahohite" here too. The Plain keeps the Hebrew "son of Ahohi" as it stands; the sense is probably the same, a man of the Ahoah clan.

a: That day the LORD won a great rescue
p: A warrior fights until his hand cramps to his sword, yet the narrator credits the LORD with the victory.
b: Eleazar fights until his hand is frozen to the hilt, and Shammah holds a field alone (23:12). In both cases the narrator says that the LORD "won a great rescue" (literally "did a great salvation"). The same phrase is used of Jonathan's raid (1 Samuel 14:45) and of David against Goliath (1 Samuel 19:5). The list of heroes does not compete with the song of chapter 22; it shows in action what the song claims: God trains hands for battle (22:35).

a: The Philistines had massed at Lehi
p: Lehi may be a place name or the word for "a troop." Chronicles has barley instead of lentils.
b: The Hebrew lachayyah can be read "to Lehi," the place where Samson killed Philistines with a donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:9–19), or "as a troop," a rare word used in 23:13. In 1 Chronicles 11:13 the field is full of barley, not lentils, and the stand is credited to Eleazar with David. Lentils and barley look different in Hebrew ('adashim, se'orim), so the change was not a simple slip; the Chronicler may have combined two stories.

a: the cave of Adullam
t: Adullam and the Valley of Rephaim
p: David's old hideout in the hills of Judah, and the valley southwest of Jerusalem where he fought the Philistines.
b: David first gathered his band at the cave of Adullam, about a dozen miles (20 km) west-southwest of Bethlehem (1 Samuel 22:1–2). The Philistines twice camped in the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem after David became king (5:17–25). This story may come from either time. "At harvest" is Samuel's reading; Chronicles has "to the rock" (see the variant). The written Hebrew here has "thirty" twice; the scribes' reading has "three of the Thirty," which fits 23:16–17.

a: the well of Bethlehem, the one at the gate
p: David, hiding in the hills, longs for water from the well of his hometown, now held by the Philistines.
b: David grew up in Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:1, 16:18). Its gate well was probably a cistern; pilgrims are still shown cisterns called "David's Wells" in Bethlehem, though the link is traditional. The scene is not about thirst alone: the Philistines held his hometown, and David spoke his longing aloud.

a: he poured it out to the LORD
p: David will not drink water bought with his men's lives. He pours it out as an offering to God.
b: Pouring water out before the LORD was a rite of devotion (1 Samuel 7:6). Blood belonged to God and was not to be drunk but poured out on the ground (Leviticus 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 12:23–24). David treats the water as his men's blood, too sacred to drink. Christian readers have seen in it an example of costly devotion and of a leader honoring his followers. The Talmud reads the story as a question of law: whether a man may take what is not his to save himself (Bavli Bava Kamma 60b).

a: with their lives at stake
p: The Hebrew is short: "who went with their lives." Chronicles and the Greek add "Shall I drink?"
b: Samuel's Hebrew is abrupt: "the blood of the men who went with their lives." 1 Chronicles 11:19 reads "Shall I drink the blood of these men, with their lives? For with their lives they brought it," and the Greek of Samuel has a similar question (in Codex Vaticanus, the kaige text; I have not checked the Lucianic text here). Many translations add "Shall I drink" to make the sentence smooth. This translation keeps the shorter text as a question, adding only "at stake" to make the sense of "with their lives" clear.

a: the two lion-men of Moab
t: Ariel: lion of God, or altar hearth?
p: The Hebrew 'ari'el is unclear. It may mean champions ("lions of God") or something else entirely.
b: 'Ari'el looks like "lion of God," and many take it as a title for heroes. Codex Vaticanus (the kaige Greek) reads "the two sons of Ariel of Moab," as if Ariel were a man (see the variant). Elsewhere the word means an altar hearth (Ezekiel 43:15–16) and is a name for Jerusalem (Isaiah 29:1–2). The Moabite king Mesha, in his stone inscription of about 840 BC, boasts that he carried off "the ariel of its Dawdoh" from an Israelite town, apparently some object of worship. Whatever the ariels were, killing them was a famous deed.

a: killed the lion inside the pit on the day of the snow
p: Lions lived in ancient Israel. The definite words, "the lion," "the snow," suggest a story everyone knew.
b: Lions roamed the Jordan thickets and hills of Israel until the Middle Ages (Judges 14:5; 1 Samuel 17:34; 1 Kings 13:24; Jeremiah 49:19). Snow falls in the hills of Judah and Moab in some winters. A hungry lion might fall into a cistern or pit, and going down after it took great courage. The Hebrew says "the lion" and "the day of the snow," as though the hearers knew the tale.

a: a striking-looking man
p: Samuel says only that the Egyptian was impressive to look at. Chronicles says he was five cubits tall.
b: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) is 'asher mar'eh, "who was a sight"; the scribes' reading (Qere) is 'ish mar'eh, "a man of appearance." Chronicles has a different phrase, 'ish middah, "a man of size": 1 Chronicles 11:23 says he was five cubits tall, about seven and a half feet (2.3 m), and that his spear was like a weaver's beam, words used of Goliath. Benaiah beats him the way David beat Goliath: armed only with a stick, he kills the giant with his own weapon (1 Samuel 17:40, 17:51).
orig: Ketiv אשר מראה ('asher mar'eh); Qere אִישׁ מַרְאֶה ('ish mar'eh)

a: David made him head of his guard
p: Benaiah became Solomon's army commander after he executed Joab.
b: Benaiah led the Kerethites and Pelethites (8:18; 20:23). When Adonijah tried to take the throne, Benaiah backed Solomon (1 Kings 1:8, 1:36–38), and Solomon sent him to kill Adonijah, Joab and Shimei (1 Kings 2:25, 2:34, 2:46). Then he took Joab's place over the army (1 Kings 2:35). The word for his post here, mishma'at, means those who obey or listen, a personal guard or council.

a: Asahel, Joab's brother
p: Asahel died early in David's reign (2:23), so this list seems to remember David's first band of fighters.
b: Abner killed Asahel in the fighting at Gibeon before David ruled all Israel (2:18–23). His place at the head of the Thirty suggests the list began in David's days at Hebron or earlier, and that later names were added. Many of the men come from towns near Bethlehem: Tekoa, Netophah, Anathoth, Bethlehem itself. A few are foreigners (23:37, 23:39). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:26–47 differs in many spellings and adds sixteen more names.

a: Elhanan son of Dodo, from Bethlehem
p: An Elhanan from Bethlehem also killed "Goliath the Gittite" (21:19). Is he the same man?
b: The giant-killer of 21:19 is "Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite." Here an Elhanan son of Dodo comes from Bethlehem. Some scholars think they are the same man, with one father's name damaged in copying. Others think the name was common. Since Dodo is also the father of Eleazar (23:9), the families of David's home town seem tightly knit in this list.

a: Mebunnai the Hushathite
p: Chronicles has Sibbecai the Hushathite here, the man who killed a giant in 21:18.
b: 1 Chronicles 11:29 reads "Sibbecai the Hushathite," and 21:18 names Sibbecai the Hushathite as a giant-killer. In Hebrew letters the two names are close (mbny and sbky), so most scholars think "Mebunnai" is a copying error. Many names in the list of the Thirty show such small differences between Samuel and Chronicles.

a: the sons of Jashen; Jonathan
p: This line is probably damaged. Chronicles reads "the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee."
b: "The sons of Jashen" is odd in a list of single men. 1 Chronicles 11:34 has "the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee the Hararite." Many scholars think "sons of" came in by repeating the last letters of the name before it, and restore "Jashen the Gizonite; Jonathan son of Shammah (or Shagee) the Hararite." The Plain adds "son of" at the start of 23:33, following the Lucianic Greek as restored in the BHS apparatus; the variant on 23:33 explains. The count of thirty-seven (23:39) depends on how such names are counted.

a: Zelek the Ammonite
