p: An Ammonite, a man from Zobah in Aram, and Uriah the Hittite all served among David's elite.
b: Zelek came from Ammon, Igal from Zobah (23:36), and Uriah was a Hittite (23:39). Ittai of Gath and his six hundred Philistines also stood by David (15:18–22). David's army, like his bodyguard of Kerethites and Pelethites, drew loyal foreigners. Several of these men took an Israelite name or served Israel's God; Uriah's name means "the LORD is my light."

a: and Uriah the Hittite
t: The last name on the list
p: The list of heroes ends with the man David had killed. Readers find the placement pointed.
b: Uriah was one of David's Thirty, a loyal soldier who would not go home to his wife while the army camped in the field (11:11), and David had him killed to cover his own sin (11:14–17). Ending the roll of honor with his name, just after Eliam (Bathsheba's father, 23:34), reminds the reader of David's worst crime at the very moment the book celebrates his men. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus does something similar: it names Solomon's mother as "the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6). Some readers think the order simply reflects the old list; others see the narrator's quiet judgment.

a: All together: thirty-seven
p: "The Thirty" was a name for the group, not an exact count. The total here includes the leaders.
b: Counting the three, Abishai, Benaiah and the names in 23:24–39 gives about thirty-seven, depending on how names like "the sons of Jashen" (23:32) are counted and whether 23:32–33 has one man, "Jonathan son of Shammah," as the Plain reads, or two, "Jonathan, Shammah," as the Masoretic Text has it (see the variant on 23:33). Some think Joab, the army commander, makes the thirty-seventh. Like "the Twelve" for the apostles, "the Thirty" seems to have been a title kept even when the number changed.

a: The LORD's anger burned against Israel once more
p: "Once more" points back to the famine of 21:1. The text never says what Israel had done.
b: The word "once more" links this story to the famine story at the start of the appendix (21:1–14), and the two stories frame chapters 21–24. But here no cause is given. Some readers think of the revolts of Absalom and Sheba, when Israel rejected the king God had chosen. Others think the narrator deliberately leaves the reason hidden, so that the story's weight falls on what David does; Rashi says simply, "I do not know" what Israel had done. Jewish and Christian commentators have often said that Israel's sin, whatever it was, was the root, and David's census the occasion.

a: He stirred David up against them
p: Samuel says the LORD stirred David up to count Israel. 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan did. How do the two fit?
b: The Chronicler, writing after the exile, retells the story: "Satan stood up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel" (1 Chronicles 21:1). Readers have explained the change in several ways. (1) Both are true: God allowed or used Satan, as in Job 1–2 and 1 Kings 22:19–23; this is a common reading, especially among Christian interpreters. (2) Satan here has no article and may mean "an adversary," perhaps human, as in 19:22 (Sara Japhet); Peggy Day argues that the Hebrew Bible has no single figure "Satan," only various adversaries. (3) Many critical scholars see a development: later writers were uneasy saying God incited a sin. (4) Others hold to Samuel's point: God rules even over a king's wrong choices, and David is still responsible (24:10); James 1:13 says God tempts no one. The Talmud ties the verb to David's words in 1 Samuel 26:19: having called God an "inciter," David was made to stumble over the half-shekel rule (Bavli Berakhot 62b). The chapter page gives more. See the chapter page and the topic on Satan.
r: 1 Chronicles 21:1; 19:22; Job 1:6–12; 1 Kings 22:19–23; Zechariah 3:1–2; 1 Samuel 26:19; James 1:13–14

a: Go and count Israel and Judah
t: What was wrong with a census?
p: The text does not say why counting was a sin. Readers have offered pride, military ambition, and a broken ritual rule.
b: Moses counted Israel at God's command (Numbers 1; 26), so counting itself was not forbidden. Explanations: (1) Exodus 30:12 required a ransom at every count to ward off plague; Josephus says David forgot it. (2) It was a draft (24:9 counts "fighting men"), a sign of trust in numbers. (3) It prepared for taxes and forced labor (1 Samuel 8:11–17). (4) The rabbis forbade counting Israelites head by head, citing Hosea 1:10 (Hebrew 2:1); Bavli Yoma 22b contrasts Saul, who counted by tokens (1 Samuel 15:4). (5) It doubted God's promise of descendants like the stars (Genesis 15:5; 1 Chronicles 27:23), which Joab's "a hundred times" (24:3) echoes. (6) Ramban (on Numbers 1:3): a count made with no need or command is wrong. Chronicles has Joab ask why it should become guilt for Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). Speiser noted census rites of purification at Mari.
r: Exodus 30:11–16; Numbers 1:1–3; Numbers 26:1–2; 1 Samuel 8:11–17; Hosea 1:10; 1 Samuel 15:4; Genesis 15:5; 1 Chronicles 21:3; 1 Chronicles 27:23–24

a: why does my lord the king take pleasure in it?
p: The ruthless general is the one who sees the danger. David overrules him.
b: Joab has killed Abner, Absalom and Amasa, yet here he is the voice of caution. He blesses the king (may God multiply the people a hundredfold) and then asks why David wants this. In Chronicles he adds, "Why should it become guilt for Israel?" and refuses to count Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:3, 21:6). Readers have noted the irony: the man David could not control was right, and the king's word "won out" (24:4).

a: set up camp in Aroer
p: The counters circle the land counterclockwise: east of the Jordan, north to Dan and Sidon, then south to Beersheba.
b: Aroer stood on the north rim of the Arnon gorge, Israel's southern border east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 2:36; Joshua 13:9). From there the census officers went north through Gad and Gilead, up to Dan and the edges of Phoenicia (Sidon, Tyre), then down through the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites to Beersheba in the Negev. The route traces the borders of David's kingdom. The Lucianic Greek reads "they began from Aroer," and many scholars prefer that to "camped" (see the variant).

a: the land of Tahtim-hodshi
p: Tahtim-hodshi and Dan-jaan are found nowhere else. Both may be damaged in copying.
b: No place called Tahtim-hodshi is known. The Lucianic Greek manuscripts, the better Old Greek witness here, read "the land of the Hittites, to Kadesh," and many scholars restore "Kadesh in the land of the Hittites," Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria (see the variant). "Dan-jaan" may be Dan, perhaps with a lost second name such as Ijon (1 Kings 15:20), or a form of Dan with an extra word. These names mark the far north of the count.
orig: תַּחְתִּים חָדְשִׁי (tachtim chodshi); דָּנָה יַּעַן (danah ya'an)

a: the fortress of Tyre
p: The count reaches Tyre and the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites, peoples who still lived among Israel.
b: Tyre was a Phoenician city on an island off the coast, and its king Hiram was David's ally (5:11). The count probably reached the border region, not the city itself. The "towns of the Hivites and the Canaanites" were non-Israelite towns within David's realm; the Gibeonites of chapter 21 were Hivites too (Joshua 9:7). Including them may mean David counted everyone he ruled, not just Israel.

a: Israel had eight hundred thousand fighting men who could draw a sword
p: Samuel gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. Chronicles gives 1,100,000 and 470,000.
b: 1 Chronicles 21:5 counts 1,100,000 in Israel and 470,000 in Judah, and says Levi and Benjamin were not counted (21:6). Explanations: (1) The two books counted different groups; some add the standing army of 288,000 (1 Chronicles 27:1–15) to Samuel's figure. (2) Numbers were easily miscopied. (3) The Hebrew 'elef, "thousand," can also mean a clan or a military unit, so the real totals may be far smaller (see the census topic). (4) Many historians think the figures are far too large for the land in the 900s BC, when archaeological surveys suggest a population of perhaps a few hundred thousand at most, and read them as an author's estimate. Josephus gives a third set of figures, 900,000 for Israel and 400,000 for Judah (Antiquities 7.320). 1 Chronicles 27:24 adds that the count was never finished or entered in the royal records.

a: David's heart struck him
p: The same words were used when David cut off the edge of Saul's robe in the cave.
b: In the cave at En-gedi, "David's heart struck him, because he had cut the edge off Saul's robe" (1 Samuel 24:5). The phrase means his conscience hurt him. In both stories David's quick sense of guilt is what sets him apart from Saul, who made excuses when caught (1 Samuel 13:11–12; 15:20–21). David also says, "I have been a great fool," words Saul used too late: "I have played the fool" (1 Samuel 26:21).

a: Gad the prophet, David's visionary
p: Gad is called both navi, "prophet," and chozeh, "visionary," David's personal seer.
b: Gad first appears telling David to leave the stronghold and go to Judah (1 Samuel 22:5). Chronicles names him with Samuel and Nathan as a writer of David's history (1 Chronicles 29:29) and says he helped set up the temple music (2 Chronicles 29:25). Chozeh, "one who sees visions," is kept distinct on this site from ro'eh, "seer" (1 Samuel 9:9). A court prophet like Gad could deliver hard words to the king who kept him.
orig: גָד הַנָּבִיא חֹזֵה דָוִד (Gad hannavi chozeh David)

a: I am laying three things before you
p: God lets David choose: famine, flight from enemies, or plague.
b: The three punishments, sword, famine and pestilence, are the standard covenant curses (Leviticus 26:25–26; Deuteronomy 28:21–25; Jeremiah 14:12). Giving David the choice makes him take part in the judgment and shows his heart. Readers have noticed that the three get shorter as they get sharper: years, months, days.

a: let us fall into the LORD's hand
p: David chooses the plague because it comes straight from God, whose compassion is great.
b: David does not name the plague; he names God's hand, and he says "us," placing himself among the people. Rashi, following Midrash Tehillim, explains the choice: in a famine those with grain stores survive, and if David chose the sword it would look as if he trusted in his warriors to protect him, but a plague strikes everyone alike, the king too. The book of Sirach (about 180 BC) turns David's words into a proverb: let us fall into the Lord's hands and not into human hands, for as his greatness is, so is his mercy (Sirach 2:18). The word for compassion, rachamim, comes from the word for a womb.

a: seventy thousand of the people died
p: Epidemics could kill huge numbers, and ancient peoples saw them as the work of angry gods.
b: Plagues swept the ancient Near East often. The Hittite king Mursili II (1300s BC) wrote prayers about a plague that killed many of his people for twenty years, and he looked for the sin that caused it. The Iliad opens with Apollo's arrows bringing plague on the Greek army. In Israel's story, plague follows the golden calf (Exodus 32:35), the rebellion of Korah (Numbers 16:46–50) and Baal-peor (Numbers 25:9). The number seventy thousand may be counted with 'elef as a smaller unit (see 24:9).

a: The angel reached out his hand over Jerusalem to ruin it
p: An angel of death carries out the plague, as the "destroyer" did in Egypt.
b: At the Passover, the LORD would not let "the destroyer" enter Israel's houses (Exodus 12:23). Here a destroying angel strikes Israel itself, and in 2 Kings 19:35 the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian army. Paul warns the Corinthians by recalling Israelites "destroyed by the destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10). Chronicles adds that David saw the angel standing between earth and sky with a drawn sword over Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 21:16), a scene the Dead Sea scroll of Samuel also seems to have had (see the variant).

a: the LORD regretted the harm
p: The verb nicham, "regret, relent," is used of God stopping a punishment already under way.
b: Nicham can mean to grieve, to regret, or to change one's mind. God "regretted" making Saul king (1 Samuel 15:11, 15:35), yet "Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret" (1 Samuel 15:29). God relents from harm after Moses' prayer (Exodus 32:14) and after Nineveh repents (Jonah 3:10). Here he stops the plague before it reaches the city, even before David's prayer in 24:17. The topic page on God's regret gives the Jewish and Christian ways of holding these passages together.
r: 1 Samuel 15:11; 1 Samuel 15:29; Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10; Jeremiah 18:8; Joel 2:13

a: the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite
p: A Jebusite still owned land just outside David's city. His name may be a Hurrian title meaning "lord."
b: The Jebusites held Jerusalem before David took it (5:6–9), and this story shows that some kept their property after the conquest (compare Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21). Araunah's name is spelled several ways in the Hebrew (the written text has "ha-Ornah," with the article, here and "Aranyah" in 24:18) and is "Ornan" in Chronicles; 4QSam-a is reported to spell it "Arna" (see the variant on 24:20). Many scholars connect it with a Hurrian word, ewri, "lord"; with the article, "the Araunah" in this verse could be a title. Together with 24:23 ("Araunah the king"), some take him to be the last Jebusite ruler. This is possible but uncertain.

a: And these sheep, what did they do?
p: David asks God to punish him and his family instead of the people.
b: David, the shepherd taken from the sheep (7:8), calls the people sheep and asks that God's hand fall on him and his father's house. Some ancient witnesses make the picture sharper: "I the shepherd have done wrong" (see the variant). Moses offered himself in the same way after the golden calf (Exodus 32:32). The question echoes the problem of chapter 21: should many suffer for one man's sin? Christian readers hear the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Jewish readers have praised David's prayer as a model of a leader taking responsibility.

a: Put up an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor
p: Chronicles says this threshing floor became the place of Solomon's temple, on Mount Moriah.
b: Samuel ends without saying so, but 1 Chronicles 22:1 has David declare, "This is the house of the LORD God," and 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon's temple "stood on Mount Moriah... at the place David had made ready: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite." Moriah is the name of the land where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2), so later tradition joined the two places. Threshing floors were flat open spaces on hilltops, catching the wind, and they were sometimes places of worship or of meeting with God (Judges 6:37; Ruth 3).

a: The threshing sledges and the oxen's gear can be the firewood
p: A threshing sledge was a heavy board studded underneath with sharp stones, dragged by oxen over the grain.
b: Farmers spread cut grain on the hard floor and drove oxen over it pulling a wooden sledge set with stones or iron teeth (Isaiah 28:27–28; 41:15). Araunah offers everything needed for a sacrifice on the spot: animals, wood from the sledges and yokes, and the floor itself. Elisha did the same when he left his plow: he sacrificed his oxen and boiled their meat on the wood of their yokes (1 Kings 19:21).

a: Everything, Your Majesty, Araunah hands over to the king
p: The Hebrew can be read "Araunah, O king, gives all to the king" or "Araunah the king gave all to the king."
b: The words are "the whole, gave Araunah the king to the king." Most translations treat "the king" as Araunah speaking to David ("Your Majesty") and make the line part of his speech. The King James Version reads "as a king," meaning Araunah gave with royal generosity. Some scholars take it literally: Araunah was the Jebusite king of Jerusalem, now giving his land to the new king (see the note on 24:16). The verb is past tense ("gave"), and some take the first half of the verse as the narrator's report.
orig: הַכֹּל נָתַן אֲרַוְנָה הַמֶּלֶךְ לַמֶּלֶךְ (hakkol natan Aravnah hammelekh lammelekh)

a: I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings I got for free
p: David insists on paying full price, as Abraham did for Sarah's tomb.
b: When the Hittite Ephron offered Abraham the cave of Machpelah as a gift, Abraham insisted on paying "at its full price in silver" (Genesis 23:9, 23:13–16). David does the same with Araunah's floor. The land of the future temple, like the land of the patriarchs' grave, is bought, not taken or given, so no one can claim it later. David's words became a byword for worship that costs the worshiper something. Chronicles has him say the same with "full price" (1 Chronicles 21:24).

a: fifty silver shekels
p: Samuel says fifty shekels of silver; Chronicles says six hundred shekels of gold.
b: Fifty shekels of silver weighed about 20 ounces (570 g), a fair price for a threshing floor and a pair of oxen. 1 Chronicles 21:25 says David "gave Ornan gold for the place, six hundred shekels by weight." Some harmonize: fifty silver shekels for the floor and oxen, six hundred gold for the whole hilltop where the temple would stand. Others see the Chronicler raising the price to honor the temple site, as he raises other numbers. Some have noticed that six hundred is twelve times fifty, as if each of the twelve tribes paid David's fifty, but that is only a guess, and the comparison mixes silver and gold.

a: The LORD accepted the prayers made for the land
p: The book ends with an altar on the future temple site and the same words that ended the famine (21:14).
b: Samuel's books began at the sanctuary of Shiloh, with Hannah's prayer and a corrupt priesthood (1 Samuel 1–2). They end with the king building an altar where the LORD's house will stand, offering burnt offerings and peace offerings, and God accepting prayer for the land. The last word is not David's greatness but God's mercy after David's sin. The story of David's death is left to 1 Kings 1–2. The Greek, in both Codex Vaticanus and the Lucianic manuscripts, adds a final note about Solomon enlarging this altar (see the variant).
